extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (philosophical anthropology/metaphysics)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length metaphysical and psychological analysis of the love of the sexes, explaining its basis in sexual instinct, its teleology toward the generation and quality of offspring, and its manifestations in human behaviour. The text offers principles about causes, functions, and differences of sexual love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love is rooted in the sexual impulse
rubrics_metrics.description: All love, however ethereal it appears, is essentially a specialised and individualised form of the sexual impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter repeatedly asserts that poetic and everyday expressions of love ultimately spring from sexual impulse; this is the foundational claim that underpins subsequent explanations of motives, behaviour, and the ‘mask’ of objective admiration that conceals sexual ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: True end of love is composition of the next generation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate and decisive purpose of love affairs is the determination of the existence and nature of the next generation—the composition and qualities of future persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This teleological claim grounds the seriousness attributed to love: individual romantic choices are evaluated by their effect on future offspring (existentia and essentia). The text treats love as the species-level will manifesting through individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct as an illusion serving the species
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature implants an illusion (instinct) so that individuals pursue species-level ends while believing they pursue their own individual good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instinct appears as an egotistical motive but objectively serves the species; examples include animals’ nesting and the human selection instinct. Instinct acts without conceptual knowledge of the end, yet produces the behaviour that realizes species goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of the species (sense of beauty) directs sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sense of the species'—manifested as a sense of beauty—guides sexual selection toward individuals who most purely express the species type: health, strength, beauty, and youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for the most beautiful individuals maintains the species' true type; beauty functions to prevent the sexual impulse devolving into mere necessity. The text links aesthetic preference directly to biological ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of passion correlates with degree of individualisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The more individualised the choice (i.e., the more uniquely suited one individual is to another), the stronger the passion; passionate love is rare because perfect mutual fit is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter defines extremes of passion and explains that higher passion arises when the prospective parents together best realise a particular individuality (father's character + mother's intellect). Poetic examples illustrate the rarity and intensity of such matches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession and physical enjoyment are primary phenomenally
rubrics_metrics.description: In conscious experience the desire for possession (physical enjoyment) appears as the immediate object of love; reciprocation is not the essential end—procreation is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that people often seek physical possession and that reciprocation alone does not substitute for it (citing suicides, forced marriages, paid favours, rape). This explains behaviours that ignore idealised romantic accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary preferences: people prefer traits they lack
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person tends to regard as beautiful in another those perfections (or even opposite imperfections) that they themselves lack—e.g., little men love big women, fair persons like dark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This complementary preference is presented as part of the sense of beauty directing selection; it explains proximate tastes and apparent mismatches that nonetheless serve species aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual adaptation/suitability determines strength and quality of love
rubrics_metrics.description: The more perfectly two individuals are adapted to produce the desired individual (in many respects), the stronger their passion and the better the resulting offspring's determinateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual suitability includes multiple qualities to be further analysed; mismatches predict unhappy marriages and inharmonious offspring. The text treats adaptation as a multi-dimensional fit (physical, character, intellect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Falling in love is the emergence of a new individual-idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment parents begin to love each other is the first appearance of a new individual (a Platonic Idea) whose germ breaks out in longing and mutual attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter uses this metaphysical framing to explain why lovers feel a fusing longing and why their efforts aim at realising that particular individuality in a child; many such germs are crushed and thus passionate love is episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual instinct can deceive and be led astray
rubrics_metrics.description: The instinct that guides sexual selection may be misdirected or degenerate (e.g., pederasty or insects misled by floral/cadaverous smells), producing maladaptive choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the blue‑bottle laying eggs in Arum blossoms and human illicit loves; these are described as instances where the sense of the species is deceived, leading to choices that do not serve optimal species ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-satisfaction disillusionment indicates species-level benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: After sexual consummation lovers often experience disillusionment because the immediate pleasure primarily served the species rather than the individual's lasting good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text points out that the vanished illusion explains why consummated love often disappoints; Plato's maxim that pleasure is vain is cited to reinforce the point that subjective expectation is illusory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male vs female tendencies: male inconstancy, female constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: By nature men tend toward inconstancy in love and desire variety after satisfaction; women tend toward constancy and retention of one mate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is explained by reproductive asymmetry: men can procreate many offspring per year, women are biologically limited; evolution/instinct thus favours male variety and female retention of a protector/nourisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnancy-related appetites as an example of specialized instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Pregnancy can produce capricious appetites in women, presented as a distinct instinctive modification to serve embryonic nourishment needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used as an illustration that women possess one more specific instinct than men and supports the claim that the ganglion (subjective) system is more developed in women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological basis: ganglion (subjective) vs cerebral (objective) systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Creatures governed largely by instinct show a preponderance of the ganglion (subjective nervous) system over the cerebral (objective) system; subjective ideas excite desire and drive instinctual behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter uses comparative physiology (insects vs humans) to argue that instinctual behaviour arises from ganglion-driven subjective ideas acting upon the brain, and that humans have fewer instincts due to greater cerebral development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic representations of love reflect an underlying truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Because artists repeatedly represent passionate love in diverse ages and cultures, the phenomenon must correspond to a genuine reality rather than a mere imaginary caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses examples (Romeo and Juliet, Werther, romances) and aphorisms (Rien n'est beau que le vrai) to justify philosophical attention to love; this functions as methodological support for treating love as a real phenomenon deserving analysis.
